planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into humus-rich, neutral to alkaline, consistently moist soil in deep to partial shade; this cultivar resents root disturbance so settle it in place and mulch lightly to keep the crown moist.

directions: This old European cultivar produces the same glossy, undivided strap-shaped evergreen fronds as the species but with margins tightly ruffled and crimped along the entire edge, giving each frond a decorative wavy border rather than the smooth edge of typical Hart's Tongue Fern. It forms a dense, low rosette and holds its leathery dark-green fronds through winter in most of its range, making it a strong textural accent among broad-leaved hostas or fine-textured sedges. It prefers limestone-influenced or neutral-to-alkaline soils, unlike most shade ferns which favor acidity, and struggles in wet, poorly drained sites. Slow-growing and long-lived, it is best left undisturbed once established.

planting.note: Set out in spring in cool, humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in full to partial shade; a limestone chip mulch or a pinch of garden lime helps replicate the calcareous soils this selection favors.

directions: A named selection from the Kaye strain of heirloom British Hart's Tongue Ferns, this cultivar bears strap-like evergreen fronds whose margins and tips are irregularly torn and fringed into narrow, finger-like lacerations rather than the smooth or merely wavy edges of the species. The deeply cut, almost feathery-edged frond outline gives established clumps a shaggier, more textured silhouette than plain Hart's Tongue Fern while retaining the same glossy dark-green color and rosette habit. It is a slow, compact grower well suited to shaded rock gardens or the base of a north-facing wall. Divide congested crowns in early spring only when necessary, as it resents frequent disturbance.

common_name: Bevis Fern (Pulcherrimum Bevis Soft Shield Fern)

planting.note: Plant in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from harsh winter winds; established plants develop a trunk-like base of old fronds that should be left in place for winter protection.

directions: Discovered as a wild sport in Devon in the nineteenth century, this celebrated soft shield fern cultivar produces extraordinarily finely divided, plumose, lace-like fronds that are sterile and reproduce true only by division, making it a slower-growing but highly prized heirloom selection. Its arching, symmetrical fronds form an elegant vase-shaped rosette with a much softer, more feathery texture than the species or most other Polystichum cultivars. It is evergreen in mild winters and the persistent old fronds insulate the crown, so gardeners should resist cutting them back until new fiddleheads emerge in spring. Best sited where its intricate frond detail can be appreciated up close, such as along a shaded path or in a woodland container.

common_name: Congested Soft Shield Fern (Dwarf Congestum Group)

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; its compact habit makes it well suited to shaded rock gardens or the front of a shade border where a full-sized soft shield fern would overwhelm the space.

directions: This dwarf, densely congested selection of soft shield fern packs the same finely cut, soft-textured pinnae as the species onto tightly overlapping, much shorter fronds, producing a compact tuft rather than the loosely arching rosette typical of the species. The crowded frond arrangement gives the plant a dense, mounded, almost moss-like texture that contrasts well against broader-leaved shade perennials. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen depending on winter severity and remains an attractive, tidy specimen year-round without staking or grooming. Because of its small stature it is easily overwhelmed by aggressive neighbors, so give it uncontested space at the edge of a shaded bed.

planting.note: Plant in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; its miniature scale makes it ideal for shaded troughs, fairy gardens, or the front edge of a woodland bed where a standard lady fern would be out of proportion.

directions: A miniature Victorian-era selection of the common lady fern, this cultivar retains the finely divided, lacy frond texture of the species but scaled down to only a few inches tall, forming a dense small tuft rather than the knee-high clump typical of the wild form. Its deciduous fronds emerge bright green in spring and die back cleanly with the first hard frost, so it is best paired with evergreen groundcovers for year-round interest. Because of its diminutive size it can be lost among larger companions, so site it where its delicate detail will not be shaded out or overgrown. It multiplies slowly by division and rarely self-sows true to type.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered through the growing season, as the crested frond tips are more prone to browning under drought stress than the plain species.

directions: One of the oldest documented lady fern sports, this cultivar produces the same soft, twice-cut deciduous fronds as the species but each frond tip and pinna tip forks repeatedly into a flattened, tasseled crest, giving the whole plant a decorative fringed outline distinct from the tapering fronds of the wild form. The crests are most pronounced on vigorous, well-fed plants and can be subtler in shaded or nutrient-poor sites. It dies back completely in fall and re-emerges as tightly coiled crested fiddleheads in spring, which are themselves an early-season ornamental feature. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor and frond quality.

common_name: Crispa Cristata Male Fern (Crested Curly Male Fern)

planting.note: Plant in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; this vigorous, tough cultivar tolerates drier and heavier soils than most fancy fern cultivars once established.

directions: This heirloom sport of the common male fern combines two ornamental traits in one plant: the pinnae are tightly crisped and ruffled along their edges, and both the pinnae tips and the main frond tip terminate in small tasseled crests, giving the whole frond a congested, decorative outline unlike the tapering, flat-pinnaed look of the species. It shares the rugged constitution of Dryopteris filix-mas, tolerating deep shade, dry shade once established, and a wide range of soil types better than many more delicate fancy fern cultivars. Fronds are deciduous, dying back after hard frost and re-emerging as fuzzy brown-scaled fiddleheads in spring. Its toughness and novel texture make it a good candidate for difficult shaded sites where showier but fussier cultivars would struggle.

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery starts once soil has warmed in spring; this selection tolerates more sun and heat than other tricolor ajugas, so it can handle a brighter exposure without scorching.

directions: Foliage is mottled in soft pink, cream, and sage green, giving a more delicate, painterly variegation than the bolder Burgundy Glow it is often compared to. Short spikes of blue flowers rise above the mat in late spring, and the clumps stay tighter and slower to spread than typical running bugleweeds. It holds its variegation and resists reverting to solid green better in warm, humid summers than many tricolor selections. Divide congested patches every few years to keep the color pattern vivid and prevent center dieback.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Herman's Pride Yellow Archangel (Clumping Silver-Mottled Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions in dry to average shade in spring; unlike the wild species this cultivar forms a well-behaved clump and will not run underground into lawns or beds.

directions: This selection was bred specifically to curb the aggressive stoloniferous spread of wild yellow archangel, staying in a neat, upright clump instead of rooting along runners. Narrow leaves are heavily brushed with silver between the veins, giving season-long brightness in deep shade, and whorls of soft yellow, snapdragon-like flowers appear in late spring. It handles dry shade under trees and shallow tree roots better than most flowering groundcovers. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the clump dense and to remove any faded flower stems.

planting.note: Install in humus-rich, evenly moist shade soil in spring; give plants a bit more room than silver-leaf lamiums since the foliage reads brighter and shows dust or splash marks more readily.

directions: Leaves are nearly solid silvery white with only a thin green picotee edge, making this one of the palest lamiums available and a stronger light-reflector in dim corners than White Nancy. Soft pink flowers appear in loose clusters in late spring and repeat sparingly into summer. Growth is a bit more restrained and mounding than older maculatum selections, so it fits neatly at the front of a shaded border without swamping neighbors. Good air circulation and avoiding overhead watering help keep the pale foliage free of leaf spot.

planting.note: Plant in part shade with morning sun in spring; a little more light than the silver-leaf lamiums keeps the chartreuse-gold color from fading to plain green, but strong afternoon sun will scorch it.

directions: Foliage is a warm chartreuse-gold with a thin silvery-white central stripe, offering a color note distinct from the silver-and-green lamiums more commonly grown. Whorls of magenta-pink flowers open in late spring and stand out sharply against the bright leaves. This cultivar can revert with occasional plain-green shoots, which should be snipped out to preserve the gold coloring. It works well as a color echo beneath gold-variegated shrubs or hostas in a lightly shaded bed.

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in part-shade soil amended with compost; trailing stems root as they spread, so space plants to let the mat knit together over one to two seasons.

directions: This older selection breaks from the usual violet-blue vinca flower color, producing soft mauve-pink blooms against the same glossy, dark evergreen leaves as the species. It spreads by trailing stems that root at the nodes, forming a dense weed-smothering mat on slopes and under shrubs. Blooming is heaviest in mid-spring with occasional sporadic flowers later in the season. Because the pink flower color is less vivid than blue forms in low light, siting it where some dappled sun reaches the bed helps the blooms show up.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide and plant clumps in spring in part shade; give this slow-establishing selection a season or two before judging its mature look, and cut back old foliage in late winter so the new white flush is not hidden by tattered leaves.

directions: New foliage emerges an unusual ivory-white each spring before gradually greening over the following weeks, giving established clumps a striking two-toned look unlike any other liriope in general circulation. Lavender-purple flower spikes rise above the arching, grass-like leaves in late summer, followed by black berries. Growth is clumping rather than running, so it stays where planted and is well suited to a specimen role among hostas or ferns rather than mass groundcover use. It is slower to bulk up than common Big Blue types, so patience and consistent light shade give the best color display.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Establish from divisions or rooted plantlets in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; because this selection rarely sets viable seed, propagation is done by division of the clump or by potting up the small plantlets it produces on its flower stems.

directions: This curiosity selection of tufted hair grass carries a genetic quirk called viviparity: instead of forming normal flowers and seed, its slender arching stems sprout tiny plantlets directly where the spikelets would otherwise be, so that by late summer each flower stalk looks studded with miniature grass babies. As the stems weight down and bend toward the soil, many of these plantlets root on contact, giving gardeners an easy, true-to-type way to propagate new clumps without division. Below the novel flower display it forms the same fine-textured, semi-evergreen mound of narrow dark green foliage typical of the species, making it equally useful as a textural filler in shaded borders and woodland edges. Give it steady moisture and part shade; because it does not spread by reliable seed the way straight species tufted hair grass can in cool, damp climates, it is a tidier choice for gardeners who want the look without volunteer seedlings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, fertile soil; this German-bred selection holds a tighter, more upright clump than the species, so it can be spaced slightly closer in mixed plantings.

directions: A German nursery selection prized for a noticeably tighter, more upright clump than the sprawling straight species, Schottland forms a dense tuft of fine, deep green foliage that keeps its shape well through the season rather than flopping open at the crown. In early to midsummer it sends up airy, finely branched flower panicles that catch backlight in a shimmering haze well above the foliage mound, a display it shares with other tufted hair grass selections but carries on a noticeably neater frame. Its more compact, self-supporting habit makes it a better fit than the species for smaller borders or mixed plantings where a sprawling grass would overwhelm neighboring perennials. Provide part shade and consistent moisture; like other tufted hair grass cultivars it dislikes hot, dry summers and performs best in cooler climates or with afternoon shade in warmer zones.

planting.note: Divide and plant in early spring or early fall into humus-rich soil; site where the heavily silvered leaves can be admired up close along a shaded path edge.

directions: Named for the influential English gardener who selected it at East Lambrook Manor, this cultivar carries broad, pointed leaves so densely overlaid with silver spotting that the leaf tissue reads almost entirely silvery-white, with only a narrow margin of green remaining at the edges. Coral-pink buds open to funnel-shaped flowers that shift through blue tones as they age, appearing atop the clump in early spring before the foliage reaches full size. The large, arching leaves hold their bright coloring and resist mildew better than many heavily-spotted selections through summer humidity. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; pair with early bulbs since the pale flowers open before most companions leaf out.

directions: This long-established cultivar is prized for the unusually soft, clear sky-blue of its flowers, a paler and cleaner tone than the violet-blue typical of the species, carried in coiled clusters above softly hairy, lance-shaped green leaves with light silver flecking. The restrained spotting keeps the foliage looking tidy and subdued through the season rather than boldly patterned, making it a good companion for brighter variegated pulmonarias. It blooms early, often among the first perennials to color the shade garden, and forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover as the season advances. Shear foliage hard after flowering if powdery mildew appears, and it will flush back with fresh, clean leaves.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 2-3 inches deep in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath deciduous trees where spring sun reaches the ground before leaf-out.

directions: This heirloom selection pairs dusky purple-pink, tubular flowers with young foliage that emerges flushed bronze-purple before greening as the plant matures, giving the whole clump a warmer, more saturated look than the plain species. Like other spring corydalis, it is an ephemeral tuber that races through bloom and seed-set in a few weeks before vanishing underground for the rest of the year, so it works best tucked among later-emerging ferns and hostas that fill the gap. Clumps thicken readily from self-sown seed and offset tubers over a few seasons, naturalizing into sizable colonies under deciduous canopy. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally rather than cutting it prematurely so the tuber can recharge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool spring weather into consistently moist, humus-rich soil; expect the clump to vanish completely by midsummer and mark its spot to avoid disturbing the dormant roots.

directions: One of the earlier introductions in this celebrated group of Chinese woodlanders, this selection produces slightly greyer, more matte foliage than sister cultivars and a long, dense succession of slender, spurred flowers in a clean turquoise-blue that is difficult to find elsewhere in the shade border. Flowering runs from mid-spring into early summer under cool conditions, tapering off as temperatures climb and the plant retreats into summer dormancy. It resents drying out even briefly during active growth, so a steady supply of moisture and a cool root run under high shade are essential to keeping the clump vigorous from year to year. Where summers stay mild it slowly forms an expanding patch that can be divided in earliest spring just as new growth appears.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture; a Scottish-bred hybrid selection valued for holding its color and vigor better than some flexuosa selections in cooler summer climates.

directions: Raised from a Scottish nursery breeding program, this hybrid produces an especially electric, saturated blue flower color set against finely divided, ferny blue-green foliage, standing out even among the other prized blue corydalis selections. It flowers over a long spring window and tends to hold its foliage a little later into summer than some relatives before going dormant, giving a slightly longer season of interest. As with other cool-climate corydalis hybrids, it performs best where summers stay mild and struggles where heat and humidity persist for long stretches. Give it steady moisture, dappled shade, and rich, free-draining soil, and divide clumps in early spring to increase the planting.

planting.note: Divide and plant in early spring into moist, humus-rich soil; an older, reliable selection that reblooms over an unusually long season with minimal fuss.

directions: A long-cultivated selection valued for its deep rose-pink, heart-shaped flowers held on arching stems above finely cut, blue-green fernlike foliage, blooming from mid-spring well into summer with far greater persistence than the wild species. The dense mound of foliage stays attractive and mildew-resistant through the season even after flowering slows, unlike many fleeting spring ephemerals in this genus. It spreads gently by rhizome to form a good-sized patch useful for edging a shaded bed or softening the base of taller woodland companions. Consistent moisture through summer keeps the foliage lush and encourages continued sporadic rebloom into fall.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or nursery starts in spring into gritty, sharply drained, humus-rich soil; performs best in a raised bed, trough, or rock garden pocket rather than heavy border soil.

directions: A diminutive alpine species from Japan, Korea, and the Russian Far East, forming a tight rosette of deeply dissected, blue-gray foliage with a distinct waxy bloom that sets it apart from the larger woodland bleeding hearts. Compact clusters of rich purple-pink, heart-shaped flowers appear just above the foliage in late spring, giving an outsized display for such a small plant. Unlike its lowland relatives, it demands very sharp drainage and resents wet, heavy soil, making it a favorite for scree beds, alpine troughs, and rock gardens rather than a typical shaded border. It appreciates cool summer conditions and light shade from the hottest afternoon sun, and it can go summer-dormant in hot climates.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil; slower to establish and spread than the common eastern species, so give it an undisturbed spot.

directions: A Chinese woodland species collected at high elevation, this Solomon's seal stands apart from its more common relatives by producing small, tubular flowers in an unusually deep purple to near-black shade rather than the typical creamy white or green, dangling in pairs beneath arching stems of narrow, glossy leaves. Its compact stature and dark, unusual flower color have made it increasingly sought after by collectors of choice woodland perennials. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form an eventual colony but takes patience compared with the vigorous common species, rewarding a shaded spot in consistently moist, humus-rich soil. Leave the rhizomes undisturbed once established, dividing only occasionally to propagate rather than to control spread.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in early spring or early fall and replant into humus-rich soil; part of the classic Bressingham breeding line alongside 'Bressingham Ruby' and 'Bressingham White'.

directions: Bred at the famed Bressingham Gardens alongside its ruby and white-flowered siblings, this selection carries dense clusters of soft salmon-pink flowers on sturdy upright stems above the large, rounded, leathery leaves typical of the genus. The bold, cabbage-like foliage takes on attractive bronze-red tones through fall and winter, giving the clump strong structural interest well beyond its spring bloom period. It is exceptionally tough and drought-tolerant once established, forming an effective weed-smothering groundcover at the front of a shaded or partly shaded border. Remove tattered old leaves in early spring to tidy the clump before new growth and flower stalks emerge.

planting.note: Plant or divide in early spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil; its smaller stature suits edging and rock garden use where full-size bergenias would overwhelm the space.

directions: This compact selection stays noticeably smaller in every dimension than typical bergenia cultivars, forming a tidy rosette of glossy, rounded leaves well suited to small gardens and container culture. In spring it sends up short stalks of clear soft-pink, bell-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, followed by leaves that pick up warm bronze-red tints as temperatures cool in fall and winter. Its diminutive scale makes it a practical choice for edging shaded paths or tucking into rock garden pockets where the coarse, oversized foliage of standard bergenias would look out of proportion. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil and remove winter-damaged leaves in early spring.

planting.note: Divide congested rhizome clumps in spring and pot into a peaty, well-drained mix; keep in warm, deeply shaded conditions with steady moisture and high humidity.

directions: Leopard Calathea produces lance-shaped, glossy dark-green leaves marked with irregular blackish-green blotches that radiate outward from the central rib like a big cat's rosettes, with a deep maroon-purple reverse that shows through when the leaves fold upward at night. It demands the same warm, humid, evenly moist conditions as its Goeppertia relatives — bright indirect light, a peaty well-drained potting mix, and consistent moisture without waterlogging — and reacts to dry air or fluoridated tap water with crisp brown leaf edges. On the Gulf Coast it performs best as a shaded patio or lanai container specimen that can be moved indoors before the first cold front, since it has no frost tolerance. Divide congested clumps at the rhizome in spring to renew vigor and produce new starts.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or set out container plants in spring after frost danger passes, in rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade.

directions: Unlike the pendant-flowered hybrid fuchsias, panicled fuchsia is an upright, woody Central American shrub that carries hundreds of small, lilac-to-rose-purple flowers in dense, branched terminal clusters rather than singly at each leaf axil, followed by small dark purple berries that songbirds relish. Its glossy, leathery foliage and shrubbier habit shrug off heat and brighter light far better than magellanica-type or hybrid fuchsias, making it a workable part-sun option in warm, humid gardens where typical fuchsias scorch. Give it rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil and afternoon shade in the hottest part of the Gulf Coast summer, and prune after flowering flushes to keep the naturally leggy growth full. It is killed by frost and should be grown as a container plant brought under cover, or treated as a root-hardy dieback perennial only in the mildest zone 9b-10 microclimates.

planting.note: Root cuttings or plant container stock in spring in a shaded to dappled-light bed with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil.

directions: Splendid Fuchsia is a shrubby cloud-forest species from Mexico and Guatemala with unusually thick, almost succulent, heart-shaped leaves that resist wilting far better than the thin foliage of typical garden fuchsias. Its flowers are equally distinctive: a swollen, pale yellow-green base tapering to a scarlet-red tip, held semi-upright rather than dangling, and appearing over a long season whenever nights stay mild. The fleshy leaves and woody stems give it more tolerance of heat, brief dry spells, and bright dappled light than most fuchsia species, though it still prefers the humidity and afternoon shade of a Gulf Coast part-shade bed or covered porch. It has no cold tolerance and must be overwintered indoors or treated as an annual outside the mildest coastal microclimates.

common_name: Bordelon Banana (Cold-Hardy Fruiting Gulf South Banana)

planting.note: Plant rhizome pups after the last frost in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, and mulch heavily over the rootball before winter.

directions: Bordelon is a fruiting banana selection that circulated among Gulf South banana growers for its unusual combination of an exceptionally cold-hardy rhizome and the ability to still set an edible bunch within a single Gulf Coast growing season. Like Orinoco, the pseudostem is killed back by hard freezes, but the underground rhizome survives winters into the upper teens Fahrenheit and resprouts vigorously each spring, giving gardeners in zone 8b-9 a realistic shot at homegrown bananas most years rather than only in true zone 10-11 climates. The medium-sized fruit is sweet and best eaten fresh once fully ripe, and the large paddle-shaped leaves supply the same bold tropical look as more tender banana cultivars. Full sun, heavy irrigation, and monthly feeding through the growing season push it toward flowering before the first fall cold snap.

planting.note: Plant near a trellis, obelisk, or large container in spring, in rich well-drained soil with roots shaded and vines reaching toward part sun to full sun.

directions: Violacea passionflower is a long-cultivated ornamental hybrid, first raised in English glasshouses in the early 1800s from South American parent species, prized for its intensely fragrant, deep violet-purple flowers with a prominent crown of fine, wavy, banded filaments. It is more compact and less rampant than maypop or blue passionflower, making it a better choice for a large trellis or obelisk rather than a fence line that needs quick coverage. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil with its roots shaded and its vines in part sun to full sun, and expect it to die back to the roots in a hard Gulf Coast winter, resprouting from the crown in spring in sheltered zone 8b-9 sites. Because it flowers on new growth, an early-spring hard pruning encourages a fuller, more floriferous vine through summer and fall.
